transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Good evening, thank you for calling S-Net Full Fibre Technical Support. My name is Gareth speaking. How can I assist with your connection?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Good evening Gareth, my name is Babatunde Adebayo. I am calling because my Fibre 900 full-fibre line is throttling down to twelve megabits every single evening between seven and eleven o'clock!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Before I look into the throughput on your Fibre 900 circuit, confirm the first line of your property address, your postcode, and your four-digit security PIN.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: My address is 42 Highfield Road, Coventry, CV2 4NZ, and my four-digit security PIN is 9410.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Address 42 Highfield Road, CV2 4NZ and PIN 9410 are verified on account 7710394821.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I pay sixty-eight pounds a month for S-Net's 'Truly Unlimited' Fibre 900 service with a four hundred and fifty megabit minimum speed guarantee, yet every night it crawls at twelve megabits!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: So to summarize your report, although you subscribe to the Fibre 900 package, your download throughput drops severely to around twelve megabits per second during peak evening hours between seven and eleven PM.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes! Twelve point four megabits down at eight thirty tonight, whereas at eight o'clock this morning the exact same computer got nine hundred and ten megabits!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let's go through the technical diagnostics to isolate the bottleneck. First, how is the computer you ran the 910 Mbps morning test and 12.4 Mbps evening test on connected to your S-Net Hub 5?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It is a desktop workstation wired directly into the 2.5-gigabit Ethernet port on the back of the S-Net Hub 5 using a shielded Cat6 patch cable.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Second question: when you ran that wired Cat6 test at 12.4 Mbps this evening, were any Wi-Fi devices, cloud backups, or television streams active on your local network?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, I deliberately switched Wi-Fi off completely in the Hub 5 admin page and unplugged every other Ethernet cable so my workstation was the sole device connected.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And what upload speed and ping latency did that wired Cat6 speed test record at eight thirty tonight alongside the 12.4 Mbps download result?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That is the bizarre part—upload speed stayed high at one hundred and five megabits per second, but download was stuck at 12.4 megabits and ping spiked from six milliseconds to eighty-four milliseconds!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: What are the optical power levels and status LEDs showing on your wall-mounted Openreach ONT box, and do you have the ONT serial number handy?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: All three LEDs—Power, PON, and LAN—are solid green, and the ONT serial number printed on the barcode label is ALCLB4409182.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Have you enabled any custom Quality of Service traffic rules, VPN tunnels, or third-party DNS settings inside the S-Net Hub 5 interface?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: None at all, the Hub 5 is on factory default settings running firmware version SG4K100174, and I tested both the Ofcom speed checker and SamKnows.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Did you also test connecting your desktop workstation's Cat6 cable directly into the LAN1 port of the Openreach ONT box using a PPPoE dialer to rule out the Hub 5 router?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, I actually tested direct PPPoE into the ONT box last night at nine PM and got 12.1 megabits down and 105 megabits up, identical to the Hub 5.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let me check the optical signal telemetry on ONT serial ALCLB4409182 right now. The downstream light level is minus 17.8 dBm, which is well inside the optimal GPON optical budget.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Right, if the fibre light level were bad, I wouldn't be getting 910 megabits at eight o'clock in the morning on my wired Cat6 desktop!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That is true. A physical fibre bend or dirty optical splice at 42 Highfield Road would degrade speeds all twenty-four hours of the day, not just between 19:00 and 23:00.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Exactly! Every single evening at seven o'clock on the dot, latency jumps from 6 ms to over 80 ms and download collapses to twelve megabits until eleven PM.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Have you rebooted both the Openreach ONT ALCLB4409182 and the S-Net Hub 5 during the 19:00 to 23:00 slowdown window to see if assigning a new gateway session changes throughput?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, I power-cycled both boxes for ten minutes at eight PM yesterday and again tonight, and the moment PPPoE reconnected it was still capped at twelve megabits.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Which Broadband Network Gateway aggregator does your PPPoE session terminate on when you look at the Hub 5 system event log?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The system log shows PPPoE session established on BNG-COV-EAST-04 with an MTU of 1492.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And how many consecutive evenings have you observed this drop to twelve megabits on BNG-COV-EAST-04?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Nine nights in a row now, ever since last Wednesday evening.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: All right, BNG-COV-EAST-04 serves the Coventry East headend exchange. I need to inspect the twenty-four-hour backhaul utilization graph for that headend link.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, please check that utilization graph because this looks like textbook peak-time exchange congestion.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Please bear with me while I query the Coventry East OLT and wholesale backhaul utilization telemetry for BNG-COV-EAST-04.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Fine, I will hold.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for holding. I have pulled the fourteen-day throughput and utilization graphs for your GPON splitter and the Coventry East headend link.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: And what do the utilization graphs show between seven PM and eleven PM?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Your local street GPON splitter for ONT ALCLB4409182 is only at thirty-two percent capacity, so the street fibre cabinet in CV2 4NZ is not congested.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, if the street splitter is only at thirty-two percent, what about the backhaul link at the Coventry East exchange?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The ten-gigabit wholesale Virtual Layer 2 backhaul pipe connecting the Coventry East OLT headend to gateway BNG-COV-EAST-04 is hitting 99.4 percent saturation between 19:15 and 22:50 every night.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: 99.4 percent saturation! So the exchange backhaul pipe is completely maxed out every evening, and that is why my 900 Mbps line drops to 12.4 Mbps!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, packet buffer queuing on that wholesale backhaul pipe is what pushes your ping from 6 ms up to 84 ms and restricts single-stream TCP downloads to around twelve megabits.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Meanwhile upload stays at 105 Mbps because residential traffic in the evening is almost all download streaming!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Correct, upstream utilization on that pipe only reaches eighteen percent during the evening peak.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Well, this is a huge relief to finally have proof of what's happening! Can you reroute my circuit onto a less congested BNG or raise an urgent capacity upgrade right now?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: No, I cannot reroute your circuit or order backhaul hardware from this desk. Exchange backhaul capacity is managed by our wholesale partner, that's their problem not mine.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Wait a second—what do you mean that's their problem not yours?! My contract is with S-Net, not your wholesale backhaul partner!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: S-Net leases the Virtual Layer 2 transit pipe at Coventry East from the wholesale network operator, and they decide when to upgrade their ten-gigabit port to forty gigabits.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Surely as my ISP, S-Net has to log a wholesale capacity breach ticket and get them to provision extra bandwidth or balance the load across another pipe!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Their automated capacity planning team reviews exchange utilization reports once a quarter, so there is nothing for me to raise from frontline support.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Once a quarter?! Gareth, my contract has an S-Net Minimum Guaranteed Download Speed of 450 Mbps, and you just confirmed on your own screen that I'm getting 12.4 Mbps every night!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Your line achieves 910 Mbps at eight o'clock in the morning on your Cat6 desktop, which proves the physical Fibre 900 profile on ONT ALCLB4409182 is provisioned at full speed.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The Ofcom Voluntary Code of Practice on Broadband Speeds measures minimum guaranteed speed during peak hours between 8 PM and 10 PM, not at 8 AM when everyone is at work!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Even so, when the bottleneck sits inside the third-party wholesale backhaul core rather than on your S-Net Hub 5, our technical desk just closes the line test as 'No Fault Found on Access Line'.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: You cannot seriously mark a 99.4 percent saturated backhaul pipe that throttles a 900 Mbps line down to 12.4 Mbps as 'No Fault Found'!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The diagnostic workflow on my screen literally says 'Access Line Pass – Downstream 910 Mbps Capable', so the automated wizard does not let me book an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I don't need a van engineer at my house in CV2 4NZ—I need S-Net's network capacity team to fix the congested pipe on BNG-COV-EAST-04 or rebate my sixty-eight-pound subscription!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I don't issue monthly subscription rebates for wholesale exchange contention from technical support, and I'm not raising a network core ticket.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: This is outrageous! Under Ofcom rules, if S-Net fails to deliver the 450 Mbps minimum guaranteed speed for thirty days, I have the right to exit penalty-free or escalate a formal deadlock dispute to CISAS and Ofcom!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: You still have fourteen months left on your eighteen-month minimum term at 42 Highfield Road, so cancelling would trigger early termination fees.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Not when you are in material breach of the speed guarantee every single night! Give me a deadlock complaint reference so I can take these BNG-COV-EAST-04 saturation figures straight to the CISAS ombudsman!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Go ahead, get lost and take it to the ombudsman then, see if I care!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Did you seriously just tell a paying customer to 'get lost' on a recorded support line?!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: You kept lecturing me about Ofcom and ombudsman rules for something controlled by the wholesale carrier at Coventry East.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I am appalled by your attitude, Gareth. I want the call reference number for today's diagnostic log on my account right now.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The diagnostic log ID generated on account 7710394821 is FLT-309481-CV, which records the optical reading on ALCLB4409182 and the gateway session on BNG-COV-EAST-04.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Does log FLT-309481-CV also record that the Coventry East wholesale backhaul pipe is at 99.4 percent utilization between 19:15 and 22:50?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, the telemetry snapshot from BNG-COV-EAST-04 showing 99.4 percent peak utilization and 84 ms latency is attached to FLT-309481-CV.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: And you are still refusing to escalate that to your wholesale network management team or log a speed-guarantee breach?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: As I stated earlier, the access line diagnostic passed at 910 Mbps off-peak, so ticket FLT-309481-CV is logged for information only.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So my Fibre 900 connection is going to stay throttled at 12.4 Mbps every single evening from seven to eleven PM with nothing done about it.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Until the wholesale operator upgrades the transit link at Coventry East in a future quarterly cycle, evening throughput will remain subject to peak contention.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I have noted your name, the time of this call, and reference FLT-309481-CV, and I will be filing a formal executive complaint this evening.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Reference FLT-309481-CV is saved on your account notes.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I have nothing further to say to you.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Is there any other technical query on account 7710394821 today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for choosing S-Net. There is a short automated survey after this call. Goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Goodbye.
